notes: Frame: PIT University Network member roster (Block A).
Captured: 2026-09-23. Register freeze date: [RECORD HERE].
Captured by: J. Kropko.
Tool: `pitun_fetch.py` v2.0.0 (saved in this directory), `fetch` then `parse`.
Registered route: member roster, enumerated in full from an archived snapshot.
Followed as registered. No gate, no authentication, no obstacle.
Three directory pages at `https://pit-un.org/directory/`, paginated
`?query-7-page=N`, 24 members per page, **72 distinct members**. Each directory
entry gives only a name, a link to a PIT-UN entity page, and a regional hub.
**The entity pages are part of the capture, not an extra.** PIT-UN lists
universities, so Rule 1 applies to every record: it resolves to the unit the
FRAME ITSELF NAMES, and the parent institution does not enter the sample. The
directory names no unit. The entity pages carry Designee, Positions,
Co-Designee, Co-Positions and Website, and those fields are the frame's naming
of a unit — for Arizona State, the positions name the School for the Future of
Innovation in Society and the Julie Ann Wrigley Global Futures Laboratory, and
the website field gives pit.asu.edu alongside asu.edu.
Capturing the directory alone would have sent all 72 records to O3 with nothing
for Rule 1 to resolve against, and Block A would have yielded nothing.
Saved: `directory/page_1..3.html`, `entities/<slug>.html`,
`entity_index.json`, `pitun_members.csv` (the frame of record, named in
`primary.txt`), `fetch_manifest.json`.
**Archived.** All three directory pages were saved to the Wayback Machine on
the capture date — separately, because `?query-7-page=N` are distinct URLs to
the archive and saving page 1 alone would have archived 24 of the 72 members.
URLs in `wayback.txt`. Unlike FORD, the site is ungated and the archive
succeeded, so the snapshots corroborate the capture rather than standing in for
it: anyone can re-fetch pit-un.org and check.
The directory snapshots cover the roster but **not** the fields Rule 1 resolves
against, which live on the 58 entity pages. A small selection of entity pages
is being archived to corroborate the specific claims in §3 and §4 rather than
all 58; the selection and its reasoning are recorded in `wayback.txt`.
- **72 members**, up from the 64 New America reported in 2023.
- **58 have an entity page; 14 do not** (see §3).
- **55 name at least one unit** in Positions or Co-Positions.
- **3 carry the International region** — Szeged (Hungary), CEPI FGV São Paulo,
and one other. C2 candidates, but C2 is a human determination at O4 from the
organization's own materials, not from this field.
- Every member that has an entity page has a usable website. The 14 with no
website are exactly the 14 with no entity page.
Fourteen of 72 members are listed in the directory but their entity page does
not resolve — the server answers with the directory itself. **Verified in a
browser, logged out, on the capture date**, so this is a property of the frame
and not an artifact of scripted access.
For those members the frame names no designee, no position, no unit and no
website. The members:
Boston University; Columbia University; Cornell University; Florida
International University; Lane College; Nazareth University; Northeastern
University; Prairie View A&M University; Princeton University; RAND School of
Public Policy; Stillman College; The Pennsylvania State University; University
of Szeged (Hungary); University of the South (Sewanee).
**No shared property explains the gap.** They are not a recent intake — Columbia,
Cornell, Princeton, Penn State, Northeastern and Boston University are
long-standing members and appear in the directory listing with normal region
tags. The group mixes large private research universities, HBCUs (Lane,
Stillman, Prairie View A&M), an international member (Szeged), and one entity
that is not a university at all (RAND School of Public Policy). The most likely
explanation is an unmaintained content-management gap on PIT-UN's side, but
that is inference and is recorded as such.
**Independently corroborated.** On 2026-09-24 a Wayback Machine save was
requested for `https://pit-un.org/entity/columbia-university/`. The Internet
Archive's crawler was served the member directory and archived that instead:
the resulting snapshot is filed under `pit-un.org/directory/`
(`.../web/20260924064248/https://pit-un.org/directory/`). A third party with no
connection to this project therefore encountered the same substitution, on the
capture date. Recorded with its requested URL in `wayback.txt`; the two must be
read together, since the snapshot alone looks like an ordinary directory save.
**A control rules out the obvious alternative explanation.** Four minutes after
the Columbia save, a Wayback save was requested for
`https://pit-un.org/entity/arizona-state-university/` and archived normally
under its own entity URL
(`.../web/20260924064606/https://pit-un.org/entity/arizona-state-university/`).
Same crawler, same session. The archive reaches entity pages when they exist,
so the Columbia result is not a crawler limitation, a rate limit, or an
artifact of how entity URLs are requested. The two snapshots together are the
strongest evidence for this finding and should be cited as a pair.
**Handling.** The records are retained — dropping them would understate the
frame's membership, which is 72 — with `entity_page_missing = TRUE` and every
entity-page field empty. `listing_text` records why it is empty. They will log
as `unit_unresolved` at O3, be counted, and feed sensitivity check (h) as part
of the bound on what the unit rule and the frame boundaries exclude.
**Why this matters beyond the count.** The register treats PIT-UN as an
identity-type frame: organizations join and thereby declare themselves. The
unit-resolution rule depends on the frame naming a unit. For 19% of members it
names nothing.
This is also a second, independent reason for excluding Block A from the
Block B to Block C unit-resolution comparison. The register's stated reason is
that PIT-UN lists universities, so the block's rate is set by a listing
convention rather than by the tradition's organizational form. This finding
adds that the rate is also set by how completely PIT-UN maintains its own
directory — likewise nothing to do with organizational form. The exclusion was
already registered; this strengthens rather than changes it.
**Consequence for Block A's yield.** Before C1–C5 and before Rule 1
resolution, the realistic ceiling for this frame is the 55 members that name a
unit, not 72. Ford is the block's other frame.
**The website is often in the anchor text, not the href.** Several entity pages
render the Website field as an anchor whose href is an unsaved WordPress
placeholder (`_wp_link_placeholder`) while the anchor text holds the real URL:
https://direitosp.fgv.br/en/...
A first pass read the href and recorded those members as having no website.
The parser now prefers a URL found in the anchor text and falls back to the
href. Any remaining placeholder or pit-un.org value is kept in its own column
(`broken_links`, `pitun_internal_links`) and `website_url` is left BLANK rather
than wrong.
Blank is deliberate. C1 asks whether the candidate has its own web presence,
and a pit-un.org page is PIT-UN's presence, not the member's. More seriously,
at O5 the lexicon proxy fetches `website_url` and pattern-matches the frozen
lexicon against it; pointed at a pit-un.org page it would compute the proxy
over PIT-UN's vocabulary and file the record in the wrong stratum for a reason
unrelated to how the organization describes itself. A blank is resolved by
hand; a wrong URL is silently believed.
**A single URL is often already unit-specific.** Brown's website field gives
`brown.edu/initiatives/data-science/home`, Case Western's `case.edu/issacs/`.
These are the frame naming a unit through the website field even where
Positions does not, and they are available to Rule 1 at O3 on the same terms as
any other field the frame supplies.
The directory and entity pages carry a regional HUB (HLC, West, MSCHE,
International) rather than a location. The hub is an accreditation or
geographic grouping, not an address, and `international_flag` is derived from
it as a signal only.
C2 is therefore determined at O4 from each organization's own materials, as
the criterion requires where a frame's location metadata is absent. Consistent
with the CTFG country-missing treatment and the CFA `location_rule` decision:
the boundary does not pre-empt a criterion assigned to a coder.
- Every record arrives `PENDING` for Rule 1, since the frame lists
institutions. Resolve only to the unit the frame names; a coder aware of a
qualifying unit the frame does not name logs it as `unit_known_not_surfaced`
and does not add it.
- RAND School of Public Policy is a graduate school inside a research
institute, so it is already a unit rather than a parent university. It will
behave differently at Rule 1 from the other records regardless of the
entity-page question — and it is one of the 14 with no entity page.
- Expect the Rule 1 worksheet for this frame to be long. That is the rule
working, not a problem.
The register asks that the 2026–27 cohort be confirmed present before capture.
**It cannot be confirmed from the source.** PIT-UN's directory does not label
members by cohort or admission year, so there is no field on the page that says
whether the current intake is included.
What is observable, on the capture date:
- **72 members**, against the 64 New America reported in 2023. Growth of eight
is consistent with continued admissions.
- The directory page's `modified_time` reads **2025-07-22** and the footer
carries **©2025**.
**Assessment recorded by the lead reviewer:** the roster is taken to be as
current as the source permits, and the stale copyright year and `modified_time`
are attributed to site maintenance rather than to a frozen roster. That is a
judgment, not a verification, and is recorded as such so a reader can weigh it.
The consequence if the judgment is wrong is bounded and is a coverage question,
not a validity one: the frame would under-represent recent PIT-UN admissions.
It would not misdescribe any member that is listed. Since the register places
population-level proportions out of scope for this strand, a roster missing a
recent cohort weakens the claim that the frame reaches the whole membership but
does not affect anything computed from the records themselves.
Two things would settle it cheaply if it later matters: a PIT-UN new-member
announcement naming institutions and checking them against
`pitun_members.csv`, or a comparison against the three archived directory pages
at a later date to see whether the roster moves at all.
**The research team is employed at the University of Virginia and is active in
PIT-UN there.** UVA is a PIT-UN member, so this frame surfaces an organization
in which the authors hold a staff role, and it does so through the frame in
which they participate.
**This is not covered by the registered Conflicts of Interest statement.** That
statement discloses one author's role at Code for Charlottesville and his
participation in the Alliance of Civic Technologists. It does not mention UVA,
PIT-UN, or the team's participation in it. The omission is recorded here on the
date it was identified — at capture, before any record was screened or coded —
and must be added to the Conflicts of Interest field in the next
preregistration update.
**What the registered procedure requires**, applied here:
- The UVA record — whichever unit Rule 1 resolves it to — is flagged
`author_conflicted` in the shared dataset.
- No conflicted author screens, codes, adjudicates or reviews the coding of
that record at any stage.
- Both research assistants code it independently, and where their codings
differ **the disagreement is reported rather than adjudicated**, because the
person who would ordinarily adjudicate is the conflicted party.
- The recusal is logged and reported with the review.
**PIT-UN itself is also implicated.** As a frame operator it enters the
candidate pool by construction under Rule 2, and the team participates in it.
This parallels the Alliance of Civic Technologists, which the registration
already flags as author-conflicted for the same reason — participation in a
network that is both a frame and a record. Treat the PIT-UN operator record as
author-conflicted on the same terms, and record that reading in the update
rather than leaving it to inference.
**So this frame yields at least two conflicted records**: the UVA member record
and the PIT-UN operator record. Block B yields two more by the same logic —
Code for Charlottesville and ACT.
**The residual limitation the registration already acknowledges applies with
particular force here.** The research assistants are supervised by the
conflicted authors, so their independence is structural rather than complete.
Independent double coding and the reporting of unadjudicated disagreement make
any resulting bias visible in the shared data; they do not eliminate it.
Readers should weigh the coding of these records accordingly.
**Action required before coding begins:** confirm which unit the frame names
for UVA (check `pitun_members.csv` — Positions, Co-Positions and Website), so
the conflicted record is identified in advance rather than recognised
mid-coding.
- [x] Capture directory and entity pages (72 members, 2026-09-23)
- [x] Confirm the 14 missing entity pages in a browser (§3)
- [x] 2026–27 cohort — assessed, not confirmable from the source (§7)
- [ ] **Confirm which unit the frame names for UVA**, and flag that record
author-conflicted in advance (§8)
- [ ] **Add the UVA / PIT-UN conflict to the Conflicts of Interest field in
the next preregistration update** (§8). The registered statement covers
Code for Charlottesville and ACT only.
- [x] Wayback all three directory pages → `wayback.txt` (2026-09-23; ungated,
succeeded)
- [x] Archive one of the 14 that redirect — Columbia, 2026-09-24; the save
returned the directory, corroborating §3 (see `wayback.txt`)
- [x] Archive a working entity page as a control — Arizona State, 2026-09-24;
archived under its own URL, ruling out a crawler limitation (§3)
- [ ] Optional: archive Brown or Case Western (unit-specific single website)
and CEPI FGV (placeholder href) to corroborate §4

Leave `location` unmapped — the frame has no location field (§5).

Frame: Ford Foundation Technology and Society grantee portfolio (Block A).
Captured: 2026-09-23. Register freeze date: [RECORD HERE].
Captured by: J. Kropko.
The register describes this frame as "manual export of the topic-filtered
view (Technology and Society, US)". No such filter is available.
What the grants database actually offers, verified on the capture date:
- The filter panel exposes **Approval date** and **Amount** only. No topic,
program, or location facet is rendered, although the page's own JSON payload
declares labels for all of them (`grantSubjectLabel: "Topic"`,
`programsLabel: "Program"`, `grantLocationLabel: "Benefiting location"`).
The facets array in the payload is empty.
- The search box matches **grantee names only**. Searching "Technology and
Society" returns 3 grants, all of which have "Society" or "Technology" in the
organization's name and none of which are in the program.
- The program appears only as a **field on each grant record**, not as
anything selectable.
- There is **no export control** of any kind.
Conclusion: the topic-filtered export the register assumes cannot be produced
through the interface. The frame was captured by a different route and the
narrowing moved from capture time to enumeration time. This is a method
deviation and is recorded for the next preregistration update. The frame's
identity and intent are unchanged: it is still Ford's Technology and Society
grantmaking.
Attempted and rejected:
- `/wp-json/ford/v1/grants` — returns 401 `rest_authorization_required`. The
WordPress REST namespace is locked. Its route index is public and shows the
grants collection accepts only `page`, `per_page` (max 100), `search`,
`orderby`, `order`, `after`, `before`, `amount_min`, `amount_max`. **There is
no program, subject or location parameter at the API level either**, which
independently confirms that filtering at capture was never possible.
- `/grant-api` — returns the ford/v1 namespace index, not grant data.
Used: **the rendered HTML documents**. The grants database is server-rendered;
each page embeds its complete JSON payload in a
`<script type="application/json">` block inside `<div class="grants-db">`. The
head carries `<link rel="next" href=".../page/2/">`, confirming server-side
pagination.
Gate: the database sits behind **Cloudflare Turnstile**. The clearance was
obtained **manually, by a human passing the check in a browser**; the resulting
cookies (`cf_clearance`, `ford_gd_ts_verified`, `__cf_bm`) were then reused for
the scripted fetch. No attempt was made to solve, bypass, or forge the
challenge. Requests were sent with the browser's own User-Agent because a
Turnstile clearance is bound to the User-Agent that earned it; the identifying
PICANTE User-Agent could not be used for this reason.
Rate: 3-second delay between requests, 44 requests total.
Tool: `ford_fetch.py fetch-html`, pagination mode `query`
(`?page=N&per_page=100`), verified before capture.
**Third-party archiving also failed, for the same reason.** A Wayback Machine
save of the grants database was attempted on the capture date and returned the
Turnstile gate, not the database. The evidence is in the resources the save
pulled in — the Cloudflare challenge widget's own scripts, carrying the same
site key as the gate markup — rather than the theme assets and embedded grants
payload a real snapshot would have fetched. Snapshot:
https://web.archive.org/web/20260924002149/https://www.fordfoundation.org/work/our-grants/awarded-grants/grants-database/
(timestamp is UTC; 20:21 EDT on 2026-09-23, the capture session date.)
This is a property of the frame, not an accident of timing, and it bears
directly on reproducibility: the gate that made scripted access difficult also
prevents anyone else archiving the frame independently. The snapshot stands as
dated third-party evidence that the database was gated on that date. It is not
an archived copy of the frame's contents and must not be cited as one. See
wayback.txt.
**Consequence: this capture is the only record of the frame's contents.** For
every other frame in the register the Wayback snapshot is a second, independent
copy. Here it is not. `snapshots/FORD/raw/` cannot be reconstructed later — the
database is live and third parties cannot archive it — so it must be backed up
off the working machine and deposited on OSF before enumeration begins.
- **4,319 unique grants**, matching the site's own reported total exactly.
- 44 pages, 100 per page.
- Year range 2011–2026.
- 2,818 distinct grantees reported by the site.
- **No filter applied at capture.** The whole database was taken; the boundary
is applied at enumeration, per `frames.json`.
The first attempt used `/page/N/?per_page=100`. The site **ignores the path
page number when a per_page query parameter is present** and returns page 1
every time. The run completed normally: 44 pages, 4,400 rows, a clean progress
bar, and a mismatch warning (4,400 vs 4,319) that read like an off-by-something
rather than total failure. Only deduplication at the flatten step revealed
**100 unique grants**, all from 2025–26 — page 1, captured 44 times.
Had this gone unnoticed, the FORD frame would have entered O3 as 100 recent
grants standing in for a 15-year database, and would have looked thin rather
than broken.
The bad capture was deleted and the tool amended: it now tests three pagination
shapes against page 2 by comparing grant IDs before fetching anything, and
stops immediately if any page contains no records it has not already seen.
**Decision: 2026-09-23, lead reviewer. The 990-PF tail is not captured. The
FORD frame is enumerated from the live grants database alone.**
The register defines FORD as a two-source frame — the live database plus the
990-PF filings from 2011 onward — on a stated reasoning: the live database
shows only active grants, so grants that closed years ago appear only in the
filings.
**The capture disproves that reasoning.** The database's own payload reports
`min_year: 2011`, and the capture returned 4,319 grants spanning 2011–2026,
including long-closed ones. Grants do not leave the database when they end. The
premise the second source rested on is false, so the source is dropped.
This is a correction rather than a reduction in scope: what is being removed is
a source justified by a property the frame does not have.
**What is NOT claimed.** We have not established that the 990-PF filings would
have added nothing. That was not measured, and the claim is deliberately not
made. What is established is that the registered justification does not hold.
**A known limitation, recorded rather than resolved.** Ford's 990-PF filings
may reach further back than the live database. The database's approval-date
facet carries a 2006 placeholder, and the register itself notes that grants
from 2006–2018 carry the "Other Grantmaking" label — both suggesting Ford's
records begin around 2006 while this capture begins at 2011. If so, dropping
the filings trades roughly five years of historical depth. That possibility was
not tested against an actual filing before the decision was taken. It is
recorded here so the trade is visible rather than implied, and so a reader can
weigh it. Anyone wishing to close it can open a 2011 filing and check whether
its grant schedule names grantees absent from `ford_grants_live_database.csv`.
**Consequences.**
- All rows carry `source_route = live_database_2026-10-01`. The `source_route`
column is RETAINED in the codebook and in `frames.json` even though it now
takes a single value, so that the filings can be added later without a schema
change and so the field's presence records that a second source was
contemplated.
- `frames.json`: the FORD `_two_source` note is rewritten to record the drop.
- Frame register (workbook sheet 2): the FORD enumeration route is amended to
the live database alone.
- This is a deviation from the registered design and is recorded for the next
preregistration update alongside the enumeration-route deviation in §1.
**Decision: 2026-09-23, lead reviewer, before any record was screened or coded.
A grant is inside the FORD frame if its program is Technology and Society OR it
carries a Technology subject.** Approximately 618 grants, collapsing to fewer
organizations once grants are deduplicated at O3.
Rule as implemented in `frames.json`:
program_slug == "technology-and-society" OR "technology" in subject_slugs
Of 400 grants Ford itself tags with a **Technology** subject:
| Program label | Technology-subject grants |
| Technology and Society | 320 |
| Civic Engagement and Government | 70 |
| Other Grantmaking | 42 |
| Future of Work(ers) | 35 |
| Gender, Racial, and Ethnic Justice | 23 |
| Natural Resources and Climate Justice | 6 |
| Creativity and Free Expression | 5 |
| Disability Rights | 3 |
| Mission Investments | 2 |
| Global Governance | 1 |
The Technology and Society program holds **338 grants, 2017–2025**. Other
Grantmaking is a residual label: Ford's program structure dates from 2018, and
earlier grants that did not map onto it carry it whatever they funded.
The registered purpose is Ford's technology-and-society grantmaking, not its
Technology and Society budget line. **80 technology-subject grants sit in
current programs other than Technology and Society** — 70 of them in Civic
Engagement and Government, which is squarely the tradition Block A exists to
cover. Those are not a labelling artifact; they are grants Ford tags as
technology while funding them from a different program budget. Discarding them
on an internal accounting distinction would mean the frame reflects Ford's
budget structure rather than its technology grantmaking.
A further **42** sit under Other Grantmaking and carry the frame's pre-2018
historical depth, which is the property Block A wanted from this frame in the
first place.
The wider boundary admits grants whose technology tag is incidental to the
organization's work. **That is what C3 (constitutive technology) exists to
remove** — take the technology away and ask whether the core activity survives.
The boundary hands that judgment to the registered criterion rather than
pre-empting it with a program label, which is the same reasoning used for the
CTFG country-missing records and the CFA `location_rule`. Expect heavier C3
attrition in this frame than in an identity frame; that is the design working.
A larger screening load, and a frame whose composition depends on Ford's own
subject tagging — which the study does not control and cannot audit. Recorded
as a limitation rather than resolved.
Both counts are reported in the write-up as a measured bound on frame
completeness: **338 under a program-only boundary, ~618 under the chosen rule.**
The difference, 280 grants, is the quantity at stake in the choice. This is the
same move as the CTFG boundary audits. The enumerator emits these counts per
run — `grants_in_program`, `grants_by_subject_only`, and
`_narrower_boundary_would_have_held` — so the bound is recomputed from the data
rather than transcribed from this note.
- Ford is flagged `lists_institutions`, so every record arrives `PENDING` for
Rule 1 unit resolution. Ford funds programs inside universities and large
nonprofits; each resolves to the unit the frame names, never to the parent.
Expect a long worksheet — that is the rule working, not a problem.
- Grants collapse to organizations at enumeration with a `grant_count`.
- Any row naming a fiscal sponsor is flagged for the Rule 1 fiscal-sponsor
clause.
- No location filter was applied at capture. C2 is a human determination at O4
from the organization's own materials, consistent with the CTFG boundary and
the CFA `location_rule` decision.
Done:
- [x] Capture the live grants database (4,319 grants, 2026-09-23)
- [x] Attempt a Wayback capture — gated; recorded in §2 and wayback.txt
- [x] Decide the 990-PF question — DROPPED, §5
- [x] Decide the boundary — program OR technology subject, §6
- [x] Map FORD's columns in `frames.json`, including `program_slugs` and
`subject_slugs`, which the boundary rule selects on
Outstanding, all blocking enumeration of this frame:
- [ ] **Back up `snapshots/FORD/` off this machine and deposit on OSF.** Higher
priority here than for any other frame, because the archive route failed
and this capture is irreplaceable (§2).
- [ ] Run `capture_log.py log` once all frames are captured
For the next preregistration update, this frame contributes two deviations —
the enumeration route (§1) and the 990-PF source (§5) — plus the
reproducibility limitation in §2. Both were discovered at capture, before any
screening or coding, and both are corrections to registered elements whose
stated basis did not survive contact with the source.

FORD's 4,319 rows will still warn as above the register's 100–300 estimate. That estimate was grantees after the boundary; you captured all grants and apply the boundary at enumeration, where roughly 618 pass. The warning is correct about the numbers and wrong about the concern

notes: Frame: Alliance of Civic Technologists member list (Block B).
Captured: 2026-09-24. Register freeze date: [RECORD HERE].
Captured by: J. Kropko.
Registered route followed without deviation, and in the strongest available
form. ACT's site is a Jekyll build whose member list is version-controlled, so
the frame is pinned to a **commit SHA rather than a date**:
repository  https://github.com/civictechnologists/website
commit      c18a8b03a798c54e0cb3ac7465b945915480a42e
file        _data/members.yml  ->  act_members.yml
This is the same treatment as CFA and, with it, the second of only two frames
in the register that can be reproduced exactly rather than approximately. The
rendered page at https://www.civictechnologists.org/about#organizations is the
public presentation of this file; the file is the capture.
**Archived at the pinned commit.** The raw file was saved to the Wayback
Machine *at its commit URL* rather than the rendered page being saved, so the
archive holds the exact bytes of the frame of record:
`.../web/20260924070442/https://raw.githubusercontent.com/.../c18a8b0.../_data/members.yml`
(see `wayback.txt`). This closes the one weakness of a SHA pin — it resolves
only while GitHub hosts the repository — without giving up the exactness a
page snapshot cannot provide. Worth repeating for CFA, the register's only
other SHA-pinned frame.
**18 member organizations.** Each record carries a name and a URL. Nothing
else — no location, no description, no delegate, no join date.
The roster itself is not reproduced in this file: it is frame contents, and
frame contents stay out of git and go to OSF. Two members are named below
because specific flags attach to them.
The repository's `_data/` directory holds `members.yml`, `organizations.yml`
and `leaders.yml`. **Only `members.yml` is the member list.**
`leaders.yml` contains unused Jekyll scaffolding — its entries are
"Mario Mario – Chief Executive Officer, Top plumber in the Mushroom Kingdom"
and similar. `organizations.yml` is likewise unused: `about.markdown` carries a
commented-out `TODO` block referencing it, which is why it survives in the
repository.
Anyone re-running this capture who reaches for the file whose name most
resembles "organizations" will enumerate placeholder content. The trap is
recorded because the correct choice is not obvious from the filenames, and
because the failure would be silent — `organizations.yml` parses cleanly.
**Code for Charlottesville is a member of ACT.** The registered Conflicts of
Interest statement discloses that an author leads and co-founded it. The record
enters the pool through this frame.
**ACT itself enters by construction** as a Rule 2 frame operator, and the
registration discloses that the same author participates in it. The
registration already flags ACT as author-conflicted for this reason.
Both records take the registered procedure: flagged `author_conflicted` in the
shared dataset; the conflicted author does not screen, code, adjudicate or
review them at any stage; both research assistants code them independently; and
where their codings differ **the disagreement is reported rather than
adjudicated**, because the person who would ordinarily adjudicate is the
conflicted party. Every recusal is logged and reported.
**To check before coding**, in light of what emerged for PIT-UN: whether either
research assistant has an affiliation with ACT or with Code for Charlottesville.
The registered procedure assumes the assistants are unconflicted coders. Where

(apolitical.co, centreforpublicimpact.org). A link with no accompanying text is

The first parse of the 2019 cohort returned 20 records with names like
*"American University of Beirut Millions of people in the Middle East…"* and
*"Rainforest"* instead of *Rainforest Connection*. The count was right; the
data was not.
Cause: the parser looked for `h2`–`h5` headings, found none, and fell back to
splitting a flattened string on a list of opening verbs. The page in fact
renders each grantee in Google's "glue" card components, which state every
field outright:
UNITED KINGDOM
Full Fact
As concerns about mis- and disinformation grow…
**This was the fourth failure of the same kind in this strand** — after FORD's
pagination, PIT-UN's entity anchors and McGovern's grantee cards. Every one had
the same cause: structure inferred from rendered text instead of read from the
page's own elements, and every fix was the same shape. The page always said
what it meant.
**Why truncated names would have mattered more than they look.** Deduplication
at O3 matches on name. Penn State and Columbia both appear in PIT-UN, and those
are cross-block multi-frame records — among the few that enter sensitivity
check (f), which requires frames from two or more blocks. A name with a
description glued onto it would never have matched, the subset would have come
up short, and nothing would have errored.
The 2019 cohort states each grantee's **country** outright in `glue-label` —
LEBANON, UNITED STATES, UGANDA, COLOMBIA. That is the best C2 material in this
frame and is captured to its own column. It is matched against a country list
rather than a leading-capitals rule, because organization names are capitalised
too: TOJIL and CIV:LAB would otherwise read as countries.
The 2025 cohort instead gives a **regional grouping** — Americas, Asia Pacific,
Europe/Middle East & Africa, Global — which is mixed in meaning: Technical
University of Munich's EMEA matches its headquarters, while Red de Innovación
Local sits under Americas and works across Latin America.
**Neither is C2.** C2 asks about headquarters or principal operations and is
determined at O4 from each organization's own materials. `listing_text` labels
the region field "as the cohort page reports it, NOT headquarters" so a coder
reading a record at O3 cannot mistake it for C2 evidence. No location filter was
applied at capture, consistent with CTFG, CFA, PIT-UN, FF and MCGV.
**Expect the heaviest C2 attrition in the register.** These are global open
calls: the 2019 cohort alone spans Lebanon, Uganda, Colombia, Indonesia, India,
Switzerland, Brazil, France, Australia and the Netherlands, and the 2026
government cohort adds Japan, Germany, Nigeria, Italy and the United Kingdom.
Several recipients are universities rather than organizations: American
University of Beirut, Makerere, Colegio Mayor de Nuestra Señora del Rosario,
Penn State, Columbia, Johns Hopkins, MIT, Warwick, Cincinnati, Nagoya, Aga Khan,
Technical University of Munich. `lists_institutions` is false for this frame —
most recipients are organizations — so records do not arrive PENDING in bulk,
and Rule 1 is applied individually at O3 where a recipient is an institution.
Note that several links already point at the funded unit rather than the
parent: `cee.psu.edu`, `transitlab.mit.edu`, `cs.mak.ac.ug`, `saferoadsai.org`.
Where the frame names a unit, Rule 1 resolves to that unit.
**The Pennsylvania State University and Columbia University both appear in
PIT-UN** — and both are among PIT-UN's 14 members with no entity page (see
`../PITUN/notes.txt` §3). They are therefore Block A / Block C multi-frame
records and enter the multi-frame subset of sensitivity check (f), which is
otherwise expected to be small. Worth flagging in advance so their
deduplication is verified rather than assumed.
Google.org operates this frame and enters the candidate pool by construction as
a Rule 2 operator, screened on C1–C5 and coded on the full instrument like any
other record, flagged as an operator, and excluded from every within-block rate
and from the saturation count because its inclusion is guaranteed rather than
sampled.
No author conflict is known for this frame.
